entities.summary:
Zuane Pizzigano, a 15th-century Venetian cartographer active in the early 1400s, etched his name into the annals of pre-Columbian exploration through his pivotal 1424 portolan chart. This meticulously crafted navigation aid, now housed in the James Ford Bell Library at the University of Minnesota, is celebrated as the earliest known map to definitively illustrate the mythical Antillia archipelago in the North Atlantic Ocean. His work stands at a fascinating juncture between medieval legendary geography and the nascent scientific cartography that would soon fuel the Age of Discovery, profoundly influencing the European imagination regarding unknown western lands.

The 1424 chart, measuring approximately 122 x 98 cm, is a parchment map drawn in the typical portolan style, featuring rhumb lines radiating from compass roses, detailed coastlines of Europe and North Africa, and conventional Mediterranean iconography. Its distinctiveness, however, lies in its depiction of four large rectangular islands situated far to the west of the Azores: Antillia, Satanazes, Saya, and Imana. These islands, rendered with remarkable detail for purely conjectural landmasses, often included place names and even specific cities, suggesting a rich, if apocryphal, narrative tradition that Pizzigano was translating graphically. This cartographic innovation provided a tangible visual representation for legends previously confined to written accounts, such as the Portuguese "Seven Cities" legend.
